weaknesses: The final Density normalization reintroduces the masking problem motivating the paper. Equation 7 gives min((1-x)A/c, 1) when zero-contribution outliers contaminate a distribution with raw score A and reference normalizer c. Whenever A exceeds c, substantial contamination leaves the score at 1. Table 4 supplies an actual example: guided DiT has A=0.63, while other rows imply c approximately 0.39. Thus approximately 38% outlier contamination can be hidden before the score decreases. This contradicts the broad claims of linear degradation and preventing good samples from masking bad ones.

Global median-radius clipping can severely penalize legitimate sparse modes, undermining the claimed separation of fidelity from coverage. In a reviewer sanity check implementing Equations 5–7, let the reference distribution be 0.9 Uniform[0,1] + 0.1 Uniform[10,110], and generate exclusively from Uniform[10,110]. With N=M=1000 and k=5, three seeds produced fidelity scores approximately 0.0015–0.0023, despite every generated sample belonging to a genuine reference mode. The balanced mode-dropping experiments do not expose this failure, and the median threshold lacks adequate justification or sensitivity analysis.

The coverage analysis does not establish the claimed calibration of the final estimator. Lemma 1 concerns the expectation of the raw statistic; applying a nonlinear inverse generally gives E[g(S)] different from g(E[S]). No finite-sample bias or concentration analysis bridges this gap. The calibration also assumes that good samples follow the reference distribution and bad samples lie outside every reference ball, leaving realistic overlapping corruptions and other distribution mismatches insufficiently characterized.

The independent benchmark substantially qualifies the headline conclusions. Tables 7–8 report failures involving sample size, hypersphere support, and disjoint dimensions. Appendix H.1 reports coverage scores of 0.947 and 0.941 for identical distributions. Figure 16 also shows appreciable parameter dependence: fidelity changes approximately from 0.32 to 0.49 as k increases from 2 to 10. These findings require a clearer account of when absolute scores are reliable; discussing two thresholds as overly strict does not resolve the broader failures.

The real-model experiments demonstrate score variation rather than establish that the resulting rankings or absolute quality interpretations are correct. There is no human, expert, or downstream-utility validation, and image evaluation relies on one embedding model. In particular, Appendix F's claim that chest-X-ray scores provide an unambiguous fitness-for-purpose judgment is unsupported. Equivalence to a reference/noise mixture alone does not validate a clinical quality threshold.

The numerical inversion in Section 4.2.2 is inconsistent as written: after sorting expected scores increasingly, the insertion index increases with the score, but g(s)=1-i(s)/M decreases. This reverses the intended calibration. It may be a transcription error, but it affects the central algorithm and needs correction, including explicit endpoint handling and an accessible implementation.
